guides.explanation_en: 国家 is the conventional word for a country or nation: a political community understood as a whole. One historical account explains its parts through the fiefs of lords and senior officials: 国 referred to a lord’s domain, while 家 could refer to a senior official’s estate or governed domain. Another scholarly account describes 家’s family living-space sense taking on a political sense and 国 and 家 blending into the compound; these accounts do not establish one certain path for every early use.
guides.caveat_en: The fief pairing is a reported historical explanation, not proof that every early use of 国家 arose directly from those two domains. Historical accounts differ in their emphasis and dating.

parts.contribution_en: In the historical fief account, the domain of a lord; in the present-day word, part of the term for a country or polity.
Historically, it could mean a senior official’s estate or governed domain, extending beyond the sense of a household; one account connects this political sense with family living space.

sources.summary_en: Describes ancient 国家 as a combined term for the fiefs of lords and senior officials, says it later referred to a country’s whole territory, and describes its modern political-entity sense. It also connects family, clan, and state with kinship and lineage organization.

sources.title: The Formation and Changes of GuoJia(國家, state & country) Idea in Ancient Chinese Political Thought
sources.summary_en: The accessible abstract of a 2015 Korean Political Science Review article characterizes 家 first as family living space associated with ancestral rites, then as political space governed by a senior official under Zhou enfeoffment and clan policies. It argues that 国 and 家 blended into 国家 during the Warring States period.

claims.text_en: In ancient political usage, 家 could refer to the stipend estate or governed domain of a senior official, rather than simply a household. The Han Dian Guoyu entry distinguishes that 家 from a lord’s 国; the specialist terminology entry similarly describes 家 as a dafu’s fief.

One specialist terminology account presents 国家 as a combined term for those two kinds of fief and describes a later extension to a country’s whole territory and then to a modern political entity. This supports a historical political contribution for 家, but is that source’s account of development rather than proof that every early use followed this path.

A scholarly article abstract gives a related but distinct account: 家’s family living-space sense became political space under Zhou institutions, and 国 and 家 blended into 国家 during the Warring States period. The current sense “country; nation” is also supported by Han Dian’s definition of 国家 as a political group and its translations.

sources.summary_en: The article's abstract distinguishes a quasi-affix 家 that can indicate a type of person from a more grammaticalized suffix 家 used after person nouns and personal pronouns. It outlines proposed grammaticalization paths for those suffix uses but does not discuss 大家.

claims.text_en: In the supplied sense, 大家 is a conventional expression for the people in the relevant group or range. The Ministry of Education dictionary glosses it as 眾人 and gives examples addressed to or involving a group.

A specialist reference treats 大家 in Du Xunhe's poem as a customary expression for the populace. The poem page identifies the work as Tang and contains the line 大家拍手高聲唱; this is a historical attestation, not proof of the modern word's derivation.

家 has documented suffix or particle uses in other expressions referring to people, and a linguistic article describes modern person-denoting and personal-pronoun suffix uses of 家. These facts make a person-reference role for 家 a possible analysis, but the consulted sources do not establish that analysis for 大家 itself.

The consulted sources do not support a distinct quantifier contribution from 大 in this word. Nor do they establish that the modern everyone sense arose compositionally from “big household,” from 家 meaning household, or from any particular older sense.

The dictionary records separate older senses of 大家, including an eminent household and a celebrated writer or expert. Their attestation does not by itself prove a historical path to the everybody sense.

sources.title: 到 — Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Frequently-Used Mandarin Words (國語辭典簡編本)

sources.title: ‘到’表结果义的‘V到X’句型历史演变研究
sources.summary_en: This study classifies 看 among modern perception verbs that occur in resultative V-到-X constructions. It proposes distinct histories for resultative constructions: a broad result use of 到 without an expressed locative complement is argued to be common by the Han period, while the resultative pattern with thought, perception, and speech verbs is traced to locative V-到-X patterns around the Song period. Its examples and analysis support a proposed constructional history, not a demonstrated derivation for every modern 看-到 phrase.

claims.text_en: In 到张飞家, 到 contributes movement toward a destination: the dictionary lists both “reach/arrive” and “go toward; go.”

In 看到, 到 follows 看 and indicates the result of that action. The dictionary describes this postverbal use as marking an action's result, and the historical study includes 看 among perception verbs used in resultative V-到-X patterns. This supports describing 到 as marking achieved perception in this example; 了 is not part of that contribution.

The historical study proposes that 到's broad result use developed from spatial endpoint uses when a location complement was absent; it argues that this bare result use was common by the Han period. The study notes that early examples without an expressed location can allow both a literal-arrival reading and a result reading, so these examples do not by themselves establish a single unambiguous historical derivation.

For the resultative pattern with thought, perception, and speech verbs, including 看, the study proposes development from locative V-到-X patterns around the Song period. Its examples include older constructions with abstract locative phrases. This supports a proposed history for the broader construction class, but does not establish the precise path by which the modern word 看到 developed.

sources.title: 傳統婚禮「拜堂」禮儀考述 — 田琛
sources.summary_en: The article surveys changing wedding rites and interpretations of 拜堂. It describes the 事林廣記 passage as a sequence of separate bows, including bows to 天神地祇, household deities, ancestors, parents and kin. sources.title: 事林廣記/前集/卷10 — 維基文庫
sources.summary_en: The text’s wedding instructions direct the newlyweds to bow first to 天神地祇 and other deities, then ancestors, then parents and relatives. This attests a ritual sequence and its objects; it does not itself show that 拜天地 was already a fixed name for the whole rite.

claims.text_en: The expression is compositionally transparent in the documented rite: 拜 names worshipful bowing, and 天地 names its object. The Chinese-Japanese dictionary specifies the object as the spirits of Heaven and Earth.
The Ministry of Education dictionary records 拜天地 for a wedding rite in which the newlyweds kneel and bow, and cites literary examples using the expression for that rite.

The Chinese-Japanese dictionary also records 拜天地 as a name for the newlyweds’ post-wedding greeting to their parents. This is a separate recorded usage; the dictionary describes worship of Heaven-and-Earth spirits in the initial wedding rite.

The 事林廣記 passage directs the couple to bow to 天神地祇 among several other objects. The research article dates the relevant material to the late Southern Song, while the quoted edition is identified as a Yuan Zhishun-era printing. This supports an account of wedding bows, not a precise date or pathway by which 拜天地 became a fixed name for the rite.

guides.explanation_en: 有 presents a calamity or adversity as occurring or being present, giving the literal sense “there is hardship.” With a person, group, or state as the subject, it means being in trouble or facing calamity. 难 is read nàn, the noun meaning “calamity” or “adversity,” not nán, “difficult.”

sources.summary_en: The page identifies the text as Song-dynasty Yang Wanli's 诚斋易传 and contains 天下有难 contrasted with 天下无难 in a discussion of hardship and its resolution.

claims.text_en: 有 contributes an existential or eventive sense here: with an event noun, 有 can present an event or condition as occurring or being present. The linguistic study describes this construction as related to existential 有, rather than reducing it to possession.
难 is read nàn and contributes the noun meaning calamity, adversity, or hardship; the dictionary distinguishes this reading and sense from nán ‘difficult.’

The combination is compositionally ‘there is calamity/adversity,’ hence ‘be in trouble; face calamity.’ 盐铁论 uses 国家有难 in this sense, and 诚斋易传 uses 天下有难 alongside 天下无难. These attestations support the compositional reading but do not establish a separate historical derivation of the modern expression.
